data.title: The FDA must stop dragging its feet  and withdraw mifepristone for abortion
data.description:
Catherine Pressly Herring was pregnant with her third child when her husband secretly slipped one of the drugs used in chemical abortion into her drinks in an attempt to cause an abortion without her knowledge. He did it repeatedly.

Catherine became violently ill and began bleeding. Her daughter survived but was born 10 weeks premature. Her husband eventually pleaded guilty to assault of a pregnant person and injury to a child. He was sentenced to 180 days in jail and 10 years of probation. After later violating a protective order, his probation was revoked and he was sentenced to eight years in prison.

In October, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration provided a court-ordered update on the safety review of the chemical abortion drug mifepristone. In it, the report release date was postponed until March 2027. The administration has been dragging its feet on needed action on the abortion pill for more than a year.

The FDA should pull the abortion pill from the market. At the very least, the administration should end mail-order abortion until a permanent solution is in place. Millions of unborn children have already lost their lives through chemical abortion, and it is far past time to act. 

In fact, the available data show the abortion pill is not safe and effective as labeled today. Chemical abortion now accounts for about 65 percent of human lives ended by abortion in the U.S., according to the Guttmacher Institute’s current national data. In 2020, the figure was 53 percent. 

Those percentages represent millions of dead American children.

The FDA approves mifepristone as part of the chemical abortion regimen through 10 weeks of pregnancy. By that point, the child has already undergone weeks of rapid development. Her arms and legs are taking shape, her fingers and toes are visible, and her major organ systems have begun developing.

The abortion pill Mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed to sustain the pregnancy. Misoprostol is then taken to cause contractions and expel the child. The purpose of the two-drug regimen is abortion: to end the child’s life.

Over the last two decades, the FDA has tragically made these drugs easier and easier to obtain. Mifepristone was originally approved in 2000 with far more restrictive rules. In 2016, the FDA extended approved use from the first seven weeks of pregnancy to 10 weeks and loosened other requirements. The agency later eliminated the in-person dispensing requirement, so that abortion pills can now be prescribed remotely and sent through the mail.

An individual can now receive abortion drugs without ever sitting in the same room as the doctor prescribing them.

There is also crucial evidence about the risks women face. The Ethics and Public Policy Center conducted the largest study on the real-world effect of the abortion pill by analyzing insurance claims associated with 865,727 prescribed mifepristone abortions from 2017 through 2023. It found that nearly 11 percent involved what it classified as serious adverse events within 45 days, including sepsis, infection and hemorrhaging. 

My organization investigated how Planned Parenthood sent out these abortion pills with no safeguards. At multiple locations across the country, investigators were told women could obtain mifepristone through telehealth without even an ultrasound to confirm gestational age. Without that screening, an ectopic pregnancy can go undetected. Abortion pills do not treat ectopic pregnancies — a rupture can cause catastrophic internal bleeding and even death.

Failure to confirm gestational age can also mean women take the drugs much later in pregnancy, increasing the risks of severe hemorrhage, infection, and other serious complications. Multiple facilities even said that the pills could be mailed to someone else’s home and kept for later use. The investigation exposed a reckless system distributing powerful abortion drugs with remarkably little medical oversight, leaving women vulnerable to dangerous and potentially life-threatening complications

Catherine Herring’s case makes that danger impossible to dismiss — nor is it by any means the only one (in the U.S. or abroad) in which abortion drugs are being weaponized against women and their children in utero by people who had no business acquiring them. Every abortion kills a baby, and in many cases like Catherine’s, it is also a crime against the mother.

Planned Parenthood’s latest annual report shows the enormous scale of its operation: 434,450 abortions during its last fiscal year and approximately $832 million in government health-services reimbursements and grants.

From the outside, it appears political considerations are influencing the timing of abortion-related decisions inside the administration. Now the election has come and gone, and the mifepristone safety report has still not been released. If election strategy shaped that timetable, it intruded on decisions that should be governed by evidence, law and the administration’s responsibility to protect the public.

And the delay continues. In its Oct. 7 court filing, the FDA acknowledged that it expects study results by mid-December, yet it does not plan to finish its report until March 2027. There are additional concerns that the study itself will be inconclusive due to a lack of Medicaid data.

Every day of delay has consequences. Women like Herring and their unborn children deserve protection now — not more bureaucratic excuses and endless delays. 

Congress must act now, because pro-abortion leadership takes control in January, and the next FDA commissioner must make a commitment to all Americans, including preborn children.

Withdraw mifepristone for abortion. At a minimum, end mail-order abortion immediately — no more delays, no more excuses.

Lila Rose is the president and founder of the national pro-life organization Live Action.

data.title: Jeffries warns Democrats ready to investigate 'everyone' in 'MAGA extremist movement'
data.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is warning that Democrats are prepared to investigate “everyone” in the “MAGA extremist movement” when his party takes control of the House in the next Congress.

“Everyone who has been part of this MAGA extremist movement that has unleashed all of this carnage and damage on the American people should be prepared to answer questions as it relates to what has happened, why it’s happened and, of course, from our view, how do we prevent this type of carnage from ever happening again?” Jeffries said Wednesday evening in an interview with MS NOW’s Jen Psaki.

Jeffries, who’s in line to become Speaker next year when the House changes hands, did not define a “MAGA extremist,” nor did he name names. But his warning is consistent with the Democrats’ promises to cast a wide net of investigations into President Trump, his Cabinet, his family and his allies when they take the gavels in the 120th Congress. 

Jeffries has spent much of the past two years accusing Trump and his allies of unprecedented corruption, including efforts to use their positions of power to enrich themselves and their families. 

But the latest warning takes on new resonance after this month’s midterm rout, which gave Democrats a huge majority with which to conduct their investigations, and Wednesday’s vote of the House Democratic Caucus, which nominated Jeffries to become the next Speaker.

Psaki, a former Biden administration official, was asking specifically about potential investigations into Elon Musk, the trillionaire tech mogul and Trump supporter who has taken steps this week to distance himself from the MAGA movement in the wake of the Republicans’  clobbering in the midterm elections.

Jeffries didn’t bite, deferring the specific targets of any probes to the Democrats who are set to chair the various investigative committees, including Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) on the Judiciary panel and Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Oversight. 

But he also pointed to Musk’s role as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency last year, when DOGE officials sought to slash trillions of dollars to federal programs championed by Democrats. 

“He was the individual who held up a chain saw and began the process of trying to detonate things like Social Security and Medicare and perhaps setting in motion what occurred in that one big ugly bill,” Jeffries said. 

Other Democrats, including Garcia, have gone a long step further, vowing already that Musk will be a target of their investigations.

data.title: Trump says he'll be more productive with Democratic Congress
data.description:
President Trump on Thursday said he thinks he’ll be more productive with the incoming Democratic Congress than he had with the GOP-led one over the first two years of his second term.

“And I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years. They’ll send me — well, they’ll send me a bill on health care, and I’ll say, ‘No way,’ and I’ll veto it. And then they’ll call me and they’ll say — and we’ll sit down. And that’s what I do,” Trump told Fox News’s Jacqui Henrich in an interview that aired on “The Ingraham Angle.”

“You’ll have them at the White House, soon?” Henrich asked Trump.

“Sure, I’ll have — I respect them, they won. Politics is a nasty game, and they won,” the president replied. “And I don’t agree with everything, but I will say this: I think I can do, in many ways, better now.”

Democrats won back the House and Senate in the midterm elections earlier this month, making notable gains in regions they have historically struggled to win, like Texas and Kansas. The GOP faced an uphill battle, with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, Trump’s slumping approval ratings and concerns about cost of living weighing heavy on voters.

Last week, Trump voiced distaste with the work of Senate Republicans, calling their actions “devastating” to the GOP and saying their lack of action caused the party’s losses in the midterms.

“The Republican Senate can no longer be the place ‘where things are sent to die.’ Not passing THE SAVE AMERICA ACT (Voter I.D., Proof of Citizenship), sent up five times by the House, was devastating to the Republican Party in the Midterms,” Trump wrote last week.

data.title: Thanksgiving dinner will come with higher price tag: Research
data.description:
The average Thanksgiving dinner will be more expensive this year, according to new research from the American Farm Bureau Federation.

The cost of the average 10-person dinner will increase by 6 percent from 2025, to $5.86 per person, Farm Bureau economists reported Wednesday.

The increase is driven by higher prices for turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries. The average price of a 16-pound turkey this year is $23.68, an increase of 10 percent from 2025, according to the Farm Bureau.

This year will mark the first annual increase in Thanksgiving dinner prices since 2022, when the average 10-person dinner cost a record $64.05 — equating to more than $6.40 per person — per the Farm Bureau.

Prices spiked in 2022, as inflation reached a 40-year high amid supply shocks and the first year of the Russia-Ukraine war.

This year, energy costs increased in the early months of the Iran war, with spillover effects for gas and diesel prices. The national average cost of a gallon of diesel fuel, which farmers and ranchers rely on to power their equipment, is roughly $5.93 as of Thursday, according to AAA. 

While that is nearly 40 cents lower than a month ago, a gallon of diesel is about $2.15 more expensive than it was a year ago, AAA reported.

The Farm Bureau also cited elevated fertilizer prices amid the Iran conflict, increased labor expenses and higher rent and electricity bills as “significant challenges” facing farmers and ranchers — who are unable to pass those costs up the supply chain, as wholesalers and retailers can do. 

In addition to higher dinner prices this Thanksgiving, Americans are also grappling with elevated gas and airfare costs. Nearly 73 million people will travel by car for the holiday, while 5.96 million will take domestic flights, AAA projected this week.  

Americans’ concerns about high costs powered a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections earlier this month, giving the party control of Congress starting in January.

data.title: Thune on midterms: GOP candidates didn't have 'much control over' key voter issues
data.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) says Republicans lost nine Senate seats in the midterms because they had no control over the issues that most impacted voters, including the Iran war, gas prices and inflation.

He also suggested the political headwinds caused by President Trump’s decision to go to war sunk GOP chances to win.

“Any exit poll that you look at would tell you it was about the war, it was about the economy, it was about inflation, it was about gas prices. I think that’s what it came down to, none of which our candidates had much control over,” Thune told John Roberts, the anchor of Fox News’s “America Reports.”

Thune noted that independent voters shifted decisively away from Republican candidates in this month’s election, something that polls shared within the Senate GOP conference months earlier showed would likely happen.

“The things that we can control going forward are to ensure that we are talking to those voters, the middle of the electorate, those independent voters who broke against us by 30 points — I mean, we lost independents, which represent a third of the electorate, in all those key Senate races by 30 percentage points,” the North Dakota Republican continued.

“We got to start delivering an economic message about the cost of living, the things the American people care about,” he added.

Thune noted Republicans can come back to recapture the Senate majority if they “win the hearts and minds of the American people.”

“That means coming up with a compelling economic message, talking about secure streets, secure borders — safe streets — and more money in your pocket,” he said. “Those are the things the American people care the most about.”

National exit polls showed that only 38 percent of voters who cast ballots in the midterm election approved of Trump’s job performance and only 36 percent said they think Trump “fights for people like you.”

The surveys also found that 63 percent of voters blamed the president for higher prices.

Senate Republicans will have a tough electoral map in 2028 as they will need to defend 19 GOP-held seats while Democrats will need to defend 16 Democratic-held seats.

data.title: Wealth taxes aren't just about who pays, they're also about who gets paid
data.description:
Proposition 40, the proposed one-time 5 percent wealth tax on California billionaires, managed to defy the political tide, crashing in defeat in the middle of a blue wave.

The fight was far from costless. And like any battle, it leaves scars.

First, there is the sunk cost of the proposed tax that never materialized. According to a Hoover Institution study, more than a quarter (28.3 percent) of those targeted for the tax, including Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, voted with their feet and left the state.

Unfortunately, this is not the first time California has experienced a billionaire exodus. The first wave of billionaire departures occurred around 2021, amid concerns over business regulation and the political climate. According to my analysis, at least 20 percent of California’s billionaire wealth left the state in the first wave, including the fortunes of Elon Musk and Larry Ellison. These departures, I estimate, were associated with $100 billion in lost economic output between 2021 and 2024, alongside reductions in employment and state tax revenue.

This illustrates a classic economic lesson: Expectations alone can produce real economic damage. Businesses and investors do not wait for a tax to become law before responding to the possibility of one. They anticipate, adjust and move when necessary, taking their investments and potential job opportunities with them.

In the end, California may have lost more than a quarter of its billionaire wealth without collecting a single dollar from the proposed money-grab. That’s a hefty price to pay.

Second, money spent on politics has an opportunity cost. The coalition opposing Proposition 40 reportedly spent nearly $380 million, while supporters are said to have spent only about $100 million. More than a dozen other propositions also were on California ballots. Overall, Ballotpedia has reported, nearly $800 million was spent for or against the 14 propositions, making it the most expensive ballot cycle in state history.

Those resources could have financed investments, funded research, created jobs or supported other productive activities. Instead, it was used for political persuasion, more than half fighting over the proposed billionaire’s tax.

Third, the campaign exposed the political tensions inherent in redistribution schemes. Many will point to the enormous imbalance in campaign contributions as one reason Proposition 40 failed. But money does not automatically translate into political victories. As election results in Texas showed, even substantial political spending by billionaires such as Musk does not guarantee victory.

The opposition to Proposition 40 was not the only source of difficulty for the yes campaign. Its own coalition was divided. Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) opposed the measure, albeit for reasons that deserve scrutiny. To prevent capital flight, he advocated pursuing a wealth tax at the national level.

But a national wealth tax would not eliminate the underlying problem; it would simply shift it from the domestic to the international arena. Wealthy Americans have already demonstrated a willingness to renounce their U.S. citizenship to avoid certain tax liabilities. A federal wealth tax would likely encourage more Americans to establish residence in tax-friendly foreign countries, bringing their bank and investment accounts with them.

More fundamentally, Proposition 40’s own design contained the seeds of its political demise. The measure allocated 90 percent of its revenue to healthcare, leaving just 10 percent for education and other state priorities. It is hardly surprising that the union behind the initiative was the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. The California Teachers Association did not support it.

This points to an uncomfortable reality about redistribution: The political fight is not just about who pays, but also about who gets the money.

Redistribution may be presented as a battle between the wealthy and everyone else, but once the money enters government coffers, competing interests begin fighting over their share. If healthcare unions receive a larger slice of the pie, less remains for everyone else. The resulting tug-of-war can fracture coalitions that might otherwise support the same policy.

Redistribution then becomes a contest over which group gets the lion’s share of taxpayers’ money.

California’s wealth tax fight encouraged capital flight, consumed enormous resources in campaign spending, and exposed the political infighting that emerges when competing interest groups fight over a prospective new source of tax revenue. There are no good reasons to repeat this at the national level.

Daniel Sanchez-Pinol is a research fellow and director of research reports at the Independent Institute in Oakland, Calif.

data.title: Live updates: Crypto leaders talk policy at Hill event; Trump, Xi, Putin issue peace declaration
data.description:
A major cryptocurrency bill remains stalled in the Senate more than a year after clearing the House, with lawmakers facing mounting pressure to establish a federal regulatory framework for digital assets.

The Clarity Act has faced hurdles ranging from partisan ethics concerns to disputes between traditional banks and the crypto industry over stablecoin rewards and decentralized finance.

That legislation will take center stage Thursday as The Hill and The Block host the inaugural Capitol Crypto Forum, bringing together lawmakers, regulators and industry leaders to discuss its prospects in the next Congress and the future of cryptocurrency regulation. The event begins at 8:15 a.m. EST.

Earlier Thursday, President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for a rare trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China. The trio issued a declaration toward peace during the discussions.

Ahead of the talks, some viewed the meeting as a poor signal of where U.S. priorities lie, while others commended the president for his willingness to have hard conversations with less friendly countries.

Meanwhile, the recent technology outages are still top of mind for many Americans. The president brushed off concerns once again late Wednesday, telling people who began stockpiling food and water to “relax.”

White House officials have ruled out cyberattacks, while experts suggest artificial intelligence-driven security updates may be contributing to the disruptions

Lawmakers are also staring down a Dec. 11 government funding deadline, with neither party settled on a strategy to avoid a shutdown. Republicans have made little progress on full-year spending bills, making another short-term funding extension increasingly likely.

Follow live below.

data.title: Trump greets Putin: 'He's my friend'
data.description:
President Trump greeted Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “friend” Thursday, as the two arrived for a meeting in China.

“Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump is heard saying, after walking into a room with his Russian counterpart.

Trump, who has long had a friendly relationship with Putin, was set to speak separately with the leader during a trip to Shenzhen, China, aside from the planned trilateral with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The talks mark their first one-on-one since an Alaska summit in August 2025, which was meant to further negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

Earlier this week, Trump told reporters that he believed the Russian president was “backing down a bit” in the war in Ukraine, which will hit the five-year mark in February.

“I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” the president said. “I think he’s backing down. I think he’d like to, frankly, I think he’d like to see it finished.”

During the trilateral meeting Thursday, the three superpowers established a “declaration toward peace.”

Back in the U.S., Republican lawmakers had mixed reactions to Trump’s coziness toward Xi and Putin.

Some have said they thought the meeting between the three leaders was a bad indication of U.S. priorities. Others said they supported an American leader who was open to having intense discussions with powerful countries.

“I’ve never been successful in getting inside the president’s head, but I can tell you where I am, we have to be more clear about who our friends are and who our allies are,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said.

data.title: Elon Musk is giving away $11 billion in SpaceX stock — and coming out ahead
data.description:
Last month, Elon Musk announced on X he wants to give away one share of SpaceX stock to every kid in America — a total of 73 million donated shares worth nearly $11 billion. But it’s hardly altruism. Donating the shares will leave Musk billions of dollars better off.

For one thing, he apparently intends to channel the shares through a tax-exempt charity, likely a charitable foundation or donor advised fund he effectively controls, and distribute them to American kids via Trump Accounts, which would give him a huge tax deduction. At a marginal tax rate of 35 percent, writing off $11 billion in shares would generate tax savings of about $3.8 billion.

But that’s only the tip of the iceberg.

Musk has already amassed hundreds of times more than that by avoiding taxes altogether. He earned spectacular investment returns not only on his own money, but also on what should have been the public’s money — i.e., money that he would have paid to the government had he been treated like the rest of us and had taxes withheld from his paychecks. Instead, he kept the float, profited from it, and compounded the profits into the stratosphere over time.

In fact, 94 percent of Musk’s wealth is attributable to his not paying taxes on unrealized gains.

Under a fair tax system, Musk would have had to account for those profits on unpaid taxes and pay them back to the government whenever he disposed of his shares. If the $11 billion worth of stock he plans to give away were held to that standard, he would owe the government 94 percent of it, or $10.3 billion.

But that’s not the system we have. Current tax rules not only allow him to avoid paying that $10.3 billion, they also provide him a charitable deduction, worth around $3.8 billion, for a combined tax benefit of about $14.1 billion — $3.1 billion more than the value of the shares he is giving away.

Musk need not be thanked for his pretend philanthropy. Instead, he should be thanking us for the massive tax giveaways lining the pockets of the uberwealthy, which the rest of us unwittingly underwrite. 

We are the ones who must pay the taxes that Musk and his ilk are exempt from, even the 73 million kids who are supposed to be the beneficiaries of Musk’s largesse. Thanks to the Trump Accounts created by the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act and new IRS rules, those kids can get a SpaceX share in their individual Trump Account, which appreciates tax-free. But when they withdraw the money after they turn 18, they will still have to pay taxes on the gains.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act required the accounts to be invested in low-cost, diversified index funds, so that children aren’t exposed to undue investment risk from a particular stock. The SpaceX stock donation arrangement flagrantly violates that rule. It requires Trump Accounts to hold the donated shares for at least five years, during which time the nation’s children will be subject to the vicissitudes of SpaceX, and assuming Musk’s proposed merger goes through, of Tesla.  

The five-year requirement is for Musk’s personal benefit: it prevents a short-term sell-off of SpaceX shares that could depress their trading price and lower the value of Musk’s continuing stake.

Could SpaceX shares tank, even when 73 million Americans are required to hold onto them for five years? You bet. Would that affect the value of Musk’s tax deduction from the donation? Not at all.

You may ask, how is this even legal? It probably isn’t, but the fix is in. On Sept. 30, an obliging IRS issued regulations tailored to allowing Musk to move forward with the stock donation without fear of effective legal challenge.

The scheme projects the misleading impression that Musk and President Trump are acting as public benefactors, when in fact they are picking the public’s pockets. Consider this alongside the record-breaking $400-plus million Musk donated for political ads and campaigns in this midterm election cycle (up from$290 million in 2024), and it becomes clear he is leveraging his vast, under-taxed wealth to further shape our society for his own benefit. 

Stephen Land is a retired tax attorney and co-host of the Fair Share podcast. Bob Lord is senior vice president for tax policy at Patriotic Millionaires, an associate fellow at the Institute for Policy Studies, and writes on tax policy on Substack.

data.title: China shuts out Bloomberg reporter for shouting questions at Trump
data.description:
China blocked a Bloomberg reporter from being in the room to cover the opening remarks of President Trump’s trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

According to the White House press pool report, the Bloomberg reporter was blocked from the event because she asked a question during Trump’s bilateral with Xi earlier in the day. 

“A Bloomberg reporter was barred from this spray because she asked a question during the bilateral meeting with Xi,” the pool report read. “A WH official said they pushed to have her reinstated but Chinese officials insisted she be excluded.” 

Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern had asked Trump during his bilateral with Xi if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been disloyal to the U.S. Trump did not respond to the question. 

The move to shut out a journalist from covering a meeting is an example of China’s restrictions on press access. It is not unusual in the U.S. for reporters to shout questions at the president and foreign leaders during on-camera meetings and events. 

Trump appeared to criticize other press restrictions during the trip earlier on Thursday. 

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it, because every move was perfectly executed,” Trump said, referring to the summit. 

The three leaders addressed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and nuclear conflict, according to text released by Russia and China.
